# Executive Summary

# Data and Exploratory Data Analysis {#initial-analysis}

In part 1 we extracted and cleaned 15-minute discharge data from the River Don at Parkhill covering ten water years (2016-2026). The threshold and independence criteria established in Part 1 are retained to identify extreme flow events, and form the basis of our analysis of hydrograph shape uncertainty.

## Robson & Reed (1999) Independence Criteria Results

Using the threshold of `r u_final` $\text{m}^3 / \text{s}$ established in part 1, we identified `r nrow(peaks)` independent extreme flow events across the ten-year observation period, corresponding to an average of `r sprintf("%.2f", nrow(peaks) / n_years)` events per year.

| Metric | Value | Unit |
|:-----------------------|:-----------------------|:-----------------------|
| **Threshold (**$u$) | `r u_final` | $\text{m}^3 / \text{s}$ |
| **Total Independent Peaks** | `r nrow(peaks)` | events |
| **Average Peak Rate** | `r sprintf("%.2f", nrow(peaks) / n_years)` | peaks/year |
| **Period of Record** | `r n_years` | water years |

## Checking the data

Before constructing individual hydrographs for each extreme flow event, we assessed the reliability of the discharge readings for each of the `r nrow(peaks)` identified events. Each event was [initially represented using a common 120-hour window](#exploratory-analysis), extending 48 hours before and 72 hours after its peak, with readings recorded at 15-minute intervals. For later analysis, we require all events to be [standardised](#standardising-the-hydrographs), forming the set of peak windows used throughout the rest of the report.

Having excluded Unchecked readings in the data cleaning section of Part 1 (SEPA quality codes 200 and 254), we identified 8 missing Unchecked readings falling within two of the standardised event windows, Events 5 and 6 (Table \@ref(tab:uncheckeddata)).

```{r uncheckeddata, results= "asis", echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(
    unchecked_model$table,
    format    = "markdown",
    align     = "llrrrrr",
    col.names = c("Burst", "Event(s)", "Start", "Readings",
                  "Duration (min)", "RMSE (m³/s)", "Max abs. diff (m³/s)"),
    caption   = "Unchecked readings (codes 200/254) within peak windows compared with linear interpolation between checked readings."
  )
```

To fix this, we compared the original Unchecked readings with estimated values to decide whether retaining these Unchecked readings was reasonable. The estimated values were obtained by linear interpolation of the nearest checked readings by assuming a constant rate of change.

```{r uncheckedscatter, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="An assesment of unchecked values"}
if (nrow(unchecked_in_events) > 0) {
  unchecked_model$plot
  
} else {
  cat("No Unchecked quality codes detected within the 120-hour peak event windows.\n\n")
}
```

Figure \@ref(fig:uncheckedscatter) compares the Unchecked and interpolated values, with a dashed 1:1 line that represents perfect agreement. Since all Unchecked readings lie close to this line with a RMSE of `r unchecked_model$rmse`$\text{m}^3/\text{s}$ against discharge values of over 30$\text{m}^3 / \text{s}$, these discrepancies are relatively small.

Although this does not prove that the Unchecked readings are completely accurate, the small size of the discrepancies provides some reassurance that retaining them is unlikely to significantly affect the hydrograph shapes.

Therefore, we retain the Unchecked SEPA readings rather than replacing them with the corresponding interpolated estimates as the values are close enough that preserving the original recorded values avoids unnecessary modification to the data.

## Exploratory Analysis {#exploratory-analysis}

To investigate the variation in hydrograph shape, the `r nrow(peaks)` independent extreme flow events are aligned at their maximum discharge, with the peak assigned time zero. Each hydrograph is examined over the same 120-hour window, allowing differences in peak magnitude, rising and falling behaviour to be compared.

```{r Hydrograph, echo=FALSE}
hydrograph_overlay_plot
```

Plotting all of the hydrographs on the same time scale shows the variation in shapes of extreme flow events. All events are aligned at their peaks showing not only do their maximum discharges differ considerably, (with the largest exceeding 400 $\text{m}^3 / \text{s}$) but the differences in the rate of discharge vary considerably.

Some events exhibit sharp peaks followed by rapid recession, whereas others have more broad hydrographs with gradual changes in discharge. Several events also display elevated discharge or secondary fluctuations away from the main peak, suggesting that extreme flow behaviour cannot always be accurately described by a single common shape.

While the mean hydrograph provides a useful summary of the typical event shape, it smooths over important differences between individual events. Consequently, representing every event using only an average hydrograph scaled by peak discharge may fail to capture the full variability in an event.

```{r heatmap, echo=FALSE, fig.height=10, fig.width=9, fig.cap="A heat map showing the varation in discharge and timeline of each of the 41 extreme flow events"}
heat_map_plot
```

Figure \@ref(fig:heatmap), illustrates this variability further, with darker shading indicating higher discharge. The concentration of high discharge around time zero is expected as the hydrographs are aligned at their maximum flow. However, interestingly there is significant variation between events before and after their peak. In particular, some events maintain high discharge for longer periods, while others return to lower flows more rapidly.

Together, both these visualisations help illustrate the variation between event shapes not captured by only their maximum discharge.

## Standardising the hydrographs {#standardising-the-hydrographs}

From our analysis above we can see that extreme flow events differ in duration, peak discharge, and the relative timing of their peaks, so without standardisation, these differences would obscure the underlying variation in hydrograph shape.

To make the events comparable, each extreme flow event was first defined between its rising and falling limb troughs. Time was then rescaled to the interval [0,1], with zero representing the start of the event and one representing its end. The relative peak position was calculated as the time from the event start to its peak, divided by its total duration.

The rising and falling limbs were then rescaled separately so that every hydrograph reached its peak at the mean peak position across all events. This alignment allows differences in the shape of the rising and falling limbs to be compared without variation in peak timing dominating the analysis.

Discharge was also divided by the event's maximum flow, giving each standardised hydrograph a peak value of one. Finally, linear interpolation was used to represent every hydrograph at 64 equally spaced points on the standardised time scale.

The resulting data were arranged into a matrix (Y), with one row per extreme flow event and 64 columns representing common time points. This provides a consistent basis for comparing hydrograph shapes and applying the statistical modelling methods described in the following section.

Importantly, the original peak discharge, event duration and relative peak position are retained separately. These quantities allow fitted standardised hydrographs to be transformed back into physically meaningful discharge and time scales for subsequent model validation.

# Methods for representing hydrograph shape

SEPA's emulator is fitted to input and output pairs of the flood inundation model, and since every additional input increases the number of runs needed to fit it, and each run is slow, we aim to keep the number of inputs as low as possible. However, after standardisation (Section \@ref{#standardising-the-hydrographs}), each of our extreme flow events $i = 1, \dots, N$ ($N =$ `r nrow(Y)`) is described by its standardised discharge $y_i(u_j)$ at each of the `r n_grid` time points $u_j$, plus its peak discharge $Q_i^{\text{peak}}$, duration $W_i$, and relative peak position $\tau_i$, giving `r n_grid + 3` numbers per extreme flow event. This is far too many to use as inputs to the emulator, so we explore the polynomial regression, Principal Component Analysis (PCA), and wavelet dimension-reduction methods from lectures, alongside two additional methods from our further reading.

Most of these methods approximate the standardised curve $y_i(u)$ by a weighted sum of $K$ basis functions,

\begin{equation}
y_i(u) \approx \sum_{k=1}^{K} \theta_{ik}\,\phi_k(u),
(\#eq:basis)
\end{equation}

and differ only in their choice of basis functions $\phi_k$. The exceptions are PCA, which first subtracts the mean curve before applying \@ref(#eq:basis), and the gamma-type curve from our further reading, which is a nonlinear function of its parameters. In every case, the coefficients $\boldsymbol{\theta}_i = (\theta_{i1}, \dots, \theta_{iK})$ for extreme flow event $i$ become our $K$ shape parameters, while the peak discharge, duration, and relative peak position are kept seperately as they are, so that event $i$ is now described by

\begin{equation}
\mathbf{x}_i = \left(Q_i^{\text{peak}},\; W_i,\; \tau_i,\; \boldsymbol{\theta}_i\right).
(\#eq:inputs)
\end{equation}

The emulator therefore only needs $3 + K$ inputs, where $K$ is significantly smaller than the previous `r n_grid + 3`.

## SEPA's Approach {#method-SEPA}

We introduce SEPA's current approach as a baseline against which every other method can be compared. Their approach treats the shape of the hydrograph as fixed, and scales it up or down using only its peak discharge.

To implement this, each extreme flow event's discharge is divided by its peak discharge and its time rescaled to $v \in [0,1]$ by its duration; however, we do not realign the peaks, as SEPA does not do so. We obtain curves $\tilde{y}_i(v)$, which are averaged across events and rescaled to have a peak value of one,

\begin{equation}
\bar{y}(v) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{l=1}^{N} \tilde{y}_l(v), \qquad \hat{y}(v) = \frac{\bar{y}(v)}{\max_v \bar{y}(v)}.
(\#eq:sepa)
\end{equation}

The fitted hydrograph for extreme flow event $i$ is obtained by stretching $\hat{y}$ to the event's duration $W_i$ and multiplying it by its peak discharge $Q_i^{\text{peak}}$, so that every event shares the same shape and differs only in its height and length. To test how well this shape predicts an event it has not seen, each event is also compared with the average of the other $N - 1$ events only. Finally, each event here is given its own observed duration $W_i$, as it is for every method, whereas SEPA's approach uses the same duration for every event, so this version of SEPA's approach may fit the observed events slightly better than the real one.

## Evaluation criteria {#methods-comparison}

Following the lectures, we evaluate each method on three criteria: accuracy, parsimony, and fitness for purpose. These are initially used to choose the number of parameters for each method (Sections 3.3-3.6) and then, to compare the methods at these choices (Section 5). 

Since flood inundation uses real flows rather than standardised ones, we first convert each fitted curve back into a hydrograph in $m^3/s$ and hours by reversing the standardisation with each event's peak discharge, duration, and peak position. Then, we compare the fitted hydrograph $\hat{Q}_i(t)$ and the observed hydrograph $Q_i(t)$ for event $i$ at the same `r n_grid` time points, and summarise error by its average absolute value across all 41 extreme flow events.

**Accuracy:** How closely each method reproduces the whole hydrograph is measured by the root mean squared error,

\begin{equation}
\text{RMSE}_i = \sqrt{\tfrac{1}{`r n_grid`}\textstyle\sum_{j}\big(\hat{Q}_i(t_j) - Q_i(t_j)\big)^2}.
(\#eq:rmse)
\end{equation}
Where possible, the errors are calculated both within and out of sample. For methods whose basis or average shape is estimated from all extreme flow events together (SEPA's approach, PCA and the choice of wavelet coefficients), we use leave-one-out cross-validation, in which each event in turn is removed, the method is refitted to the remaining $N - 1$ events, and the removed event is predicted. For methods fitted to each event separately (polynomial, B-spline and gamma-type), leaving an event out does not change the fit to the others, so the in-sample and leave-one-out errors are identical; for these, the events were instead split once at random into `r length(train_floods)` training and `r length(test_floods)` test events, which is used to choose each method's settings.

**Parsimony:** The number of parameters needed to achieve that accuracy matters because the parameters become the emulator's inputs, and fewer, less correlated parameters make both the emulator and the modelling of their uncertainty easier. We therefore compare the number of shape parameters of each method and the correlation between them across events.

**Fitness for purpose:** A small RMSE can hide a poorly fitted peak, so we also measure how well each method reconstructs the features of the hydrograph that matter most for flooding,

\begin{align}
\text{Peak error}_i &= \max_j \hat{Q}_i(t_j) - \max_j Q_i(t_j), (\#eq:peak)\\
\text{Timing error}_i &= \hat{t}_{i}^{\,\text{peak}} - t_{i}^{\,\text{peak}}, (\#eq:timing)\\
\text{Volume error}_i &= 100 \times \frac{\int \hat{Q}_i(t)\,dt - \int Q_i(t)\,dt}{\int Q_i(t)\,dt}\ \%, (\#eq:volume)
\end{align}
where the integrals are evaluated by the trapezium rule. The peak discharge determines the maximum extent of an extreme flow event, and the total volume of water affects how long the event lasts. As every method except SEPA's places the peak at its observed position, their timing errors are close to zero by construction, so this error is mainly informative for the baseline. We also consider how well unusual events are captured. The second part of fitness for purpose, whether the parameters produce sensible hydrographs when used to simulate new events, can only be assessed once their uncertainty has been modelled, and also provides the genuine out-of-sample test for methods fitted to each event separately (Section \@ref(uncertainty)).

## Polynomial regression {#method-polynomial}

First, we consider a polynomial in time as our choice of basis, so that the standardised hydrograph of event $i$ is approximated by

\begin{equation}
y_i(u_j) \approx \theta_{i0} + \theta_{i1}u_j + \theta_{i2}u_j^2 + \dots + \theta_{ip}u_j^p, \qquad j = 1, \dots, `r n_grid`.
(\#eq:poly)
\end{equation}
Since this is a linear model, the coefficients are found by least squares as $\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_i = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top \mathbf{y}_i$, where $X$ is the `r n_grid` $\times (p+1)$ matrix with columns $1, u, \dots, u^p$ evaluated at the grid times, and $\mathbf{y}_i$ is the standardised curve of event $i$. The $p + 1$ fitted coefficients are the shape parameters of the event.

To choose the degree $p$, we considered degrees from `r min(degrees)` to `r max(degrees)` in two ways. First, for each degree, we recorded the proportion of events for which the highest-order term was significant at the 5% level (Table \@ref(tab:polysig)). However, neighbouring points on a hydrograph are strongly correlated, which violates the independence assumption of the linear model, so the standard errors are too small and these tests too optimistic, and they were therefore used only as a guide. Second, we compared the errors for each degree across the training and test events (Section \@ref(methods-comparison), Figure \@ref(fig:polychoice)).

```{r polysig, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(degree = degrees, prop = sprintf("%.2f", prop_significant)),
  format    = "markdown",
  col.names = c("Degree $p$", "Proportion of events with $\\theta_p$ significant at 5%"),
  align     = "cc",
  caption   = "Proportion of events for which the highest-order polynomial term is significant at the 5% level."
)
```

```{r polychoice, echo=FALSE, fig.height=6, fig.cap="Average absolute errors for training and test events by polynomial degree."}
plot_choice(poly_choice, "Polynomial degree")
```

We observe that the proportion of significant highest-order terms does not decrease steadily with the degree, but is much higher at odd degrees than at even ones, and that every error continues to fall as the degree increases, with the test errors following the training errors closely. The largest improvements also occur when moving to an odd degree, with the step from degree 6 to 7 giving the largest single reduction in the peak error, while further increases give smaller gains for each additional parameter, so we chose $p =$ `r p_chosen`. Additionally, degree 8 gave similar errors, whereas degree 6 was noticeably less accurate at the peak, so the choice is not sensitive to a small increase in $p$.

## Principal component analysis {#method-pca}

Unlike the polynomial, where the basis is fixed before looking at the data, PCA estimates the basis from the extreme flow events themselves, finding the curves that best describe how the events differ from one another. To do this, we arrange the standardised hydrographs into the `r nrow(Y)` $\times$ `r n_grid` matrix $Y$, with one row per event, and centre each column by subtracting the mean curve $\bar{y}(u_j)$. We do not scale the columns, as every column is already on the same standardised scale. PCA then finds the principal components $\phi_1, \phi_2, \dots$, which are the eigenvectors of the sample covariance matrix of $Y$, ordered so that the first explains the most variation between events, the second the most of what remains, and so on. Each standardised hydrograph is then approximated by

\begin{equation}
y_i(u_j) \approx \bar{y}(u_j) + \sum_{k=1}^{K} \xi_{ik}\,\phi_k(u_j), \qquad \xi_{ik} = \sum_{j=1}^{`r n_grid`} \big(y_i(u_j) - \bar{y}(u_j)\big)\,\phi_k(u_j),
(\#eq:pca)
\end{equation}
where the scores $\xi_{i1}, \dots, \xi_{iK}$ are the shape parameters of event $i$. An advantage of PCA is that the scores of different components are uncorrelated across events by construction, which makes their variation between events easier to model.

```{r pcaloadings, echo=FALSE, fig.height=4, fig.cap="The first three principal components against standardised time."}
matplot(grid_u, pca_result$rotation[, 1:3], type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 2,
        col = c("#AA1945", "#5298BC", "#174B67"),
        xlab = "Standardised time u", ylab = "Loading", main = "")
abline(h = 0, lty = 3)
legend("bottomright", c("PC1", "PC2", "PC3"), lty = 1, lwd = 2,
       col = c("#AA1945", "#5298BC", "#174B67"), bty = "n")
```

Figure \@ref(fig:pcaloadings) shows the first three principal components, which together explain `r round(100 * cum_var[3])`% of the variation between events. We observe that all three are close to zero at the peak, $u^\ast =$ `r round(u_star, 2)`, since every standardised hydrograph has the same value there. The first component, which alone explains `r round(100 * cum_var[1])`% of the variation, has the same sign on both sides of the peak, and so describes how broad the event is, that is, how high the flow stays relative to the peak, particularly on the rising limb. The second component has opposite signs before and after the peak, and so contrasts the flow shortly before the peak with the flow during the recession. The third component is concentrated on the rising limb, and describes how late and how steeply the flow rises towards the peak, which also captures events with an earlier, smaller peak.

To choose the number of components $K$, we again considered two approaches. First, we plotted the cumulative proportion of the variation explained against $K$ (Figure \@ref(fig:pcacumvar)), where the common rule of explaining 95% of the variation gives $K =$ `r which(cum_var >= 0.95)[1]`. Second, since the components are estimated from all events together, we compared the in-sample and leave-one-out errors for each $K$ (Section \@ref(methods-comparison), Figure \@ref(fig:pcachoice)), recalculating the mean curve and components without each left-out event before reconstructing it. We observe that the RMSE and volume error fall as $K$ increases, with the leave-one-out errors only slightly above the in-sample errors, so the components found from the other events generalise well to a new event. Moving from 6 to 7 components gives almost no improvement in the leave-one-out RMSE, so, in agreement with the 95% rule, we chose $K =$ `r k_chosen`. We also observe that the peak and timing errors are very small for every $K$, at under 1 m³/s and 1 hour, since the variation between events at the peak is almost zero, so the mean curve already reproduces the peak.

```{r pcacumvar, echo=FALSE, fig.height=4, fig.cap="Cumulative proportion of variation explained by the first $K$ principal components, with the dashed line at 95%."}
plot(seq_along(cum_var), cum_var, type = "b", pch = 19,
     xlab = "Number of components K", ylab = "Cumulative proportion of variation")
abline(h = 0.95, lty = 2, col = "#AA1945")
```

```{r pcachoice, echo=FALSE, fig.height=6, fig.cap="Average absolute errors, in-sample and leave-one-out, by number of principal components."}
plot_choice(pca_choice, "Number of components K")
```

## Wavelets {#method-wavelets}

Finally, we consider wavelets. A wavelet is a short, localised wave that starts at zero, oscillates briefly and returns to zero, and a hydrograph can be built up from shifted and stretched copies of a single wavelet, each describing the detail in the curve at a particular time and scale. This makes wavelets potentially well suited to hydrographs, which are often dominated by a single sharp peak that may be described by only a few of them. As for the polynomial, the basis is fixed and fitted to each extreme flow event separately, but here using wavelet functions in place of powers of time.

Using the discrete wavelet transform, each standardised hydrograph is split into a smooth trend and the detail at `r wav_levels` successively coarser scales, so that

\begin{equation}
y_i(u) = \sum_{k} a_{ik}\,\varphi_k(u) + \sum_{j=1}^{`r wav_levels`}\sum_{k} d_{ijk}\,\psi_{jk}(u),
(\#eq:wavelet)
\end{equation}
where the $a_{ik}$ are the smooth coefficients, describing the overall shape of the hydrograph, and the $d_{ijk}$ are the detail coefficients at scale $j$ and location $k$, with $j = 1$ the finest scale. We used the Daubechies wavelet with four coefficients, `r wav_levels` levels and periodic boundaries, and since `r n_grid` $= 2^6$, the transform can be applied to each hydrograph directly. With these settings, each hydrograph has `r n_grid / 2^wav_levels` smooth coefficients and `r n_grid - n_grid / 2^wav_levels` detail coefficients, so that using all of them would reproduce the hydrograph exactly. Figure \@ref(fig:wavdecomp) shows this decomposition for event 1, where we observe that the smooth coefficients capture the overall shape of the event, while the detail coefficients are close to zero except around the peak, and are smallest at the finest scale.

```{r wavdecomp, echo=FALSE, fig.height=6, fig.cap="Wavelet decomposition of event 1: the detail coefficients at each level and the smooth coefficients."}
par(mfrow = c(4, 1), mar = c(2, 4, 2, 1))
plot(wt_example@W[[1]], type = "h", lwd = 2, col = "#5298BC", xlab = "", ylab = "", main = "Level 1 detail (finest)")
plot(wt_example@W[[2]], type = "h", lwd = 2, col = "#5298BC", xlab = "", ylab = "", main = "Level 2 detail")
plot(wt_example@W[[3]], type = "h", lwd = 2, col = "#5298BC", xlab = "", ylab = "", main = "Level 3 detail (coarsest)")
plot(wt_example@V[[3]], type = "h", lwd = 2, col = "#174B67", xlab = "", ylab = "", main = "Level 3 smooth")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1), mar = c(5, 4, 4, 2) + 0.1)
```

To reduce the number of parameters, we keep all of the smooth coefficients but only the $M$ detail coefficients that are largest on average across events, setting the rest to zero. The same $M$ coefficients are kept for every event, so that all events share the same basis, and the shape parameters of each event are its `r n_grid / 2^wav_levels` smooth coefficients and $M$ kept detail coefficients. To choose $M$, we compared the in-sample and leave-one-out errors for different values of $M$ (Section \@ref(methods-comparison), Figure \@ref(fig:wavchoice)), where for each left-out event the coefficients to keep are chosen from the remaining events only. We observe that the leave-one-out errors are almost identical to the in-sample errors, since leaving out one event barely changes which coefficients are largest on average. The peak error falls sharply up to $M = 5$ and then stays roughly constant up to $M = 10$, while the RMSE continues to fall more gradually and the volume error stays below 0.25% throughout. Since each additional coefficient adds a parameter, we chose $M =$ `r keep_chosen`, giving `r ncol(wav_params)` shape parameters per event.

```{r wavchoice, echo=FALSE, fig.height=6, fig.cap="Average absolute errors, in-sample and leave-one-out, by number of detail coefficients kept."}
plot_choice(wav_choice, "Detail coefficients kept")
```

We also checked the sensitivity of the results to the choice of wavelet and the number of levels, keeping $M =$ `r keep_chosen` fixed (Table \@ref(tab:wavsens)). Since more levels give fewer smooth coefficients, this also changes the number of parameters. We observe that the number of levels matters much more than the choice of wavelet, with the RMSE, peak and volume errors all increasing as the number of levels increases and the number of parameters falls, from 13 parameters at three levels to 7 at five levels. For a given number of levels, the Haar wavelet has a noticeably higher RMSE than the two Daubechies wavelets. The least asymmetric Daubechies wavelet with eight coefficients has a similar RMSE to our choice, and a lower peak error at three levels (0.90 compared with 2.96 m³/s), but we kept the Daubechies wavelet with four coefficients used in the lecture example, as the difference at the peak is small compared with the other methods.

```{r wavsens, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(
  wav_sensitivity, digits = 2, format = "markdown",
  col.names = c("Wavelet", "Levels", "Shape parameters", "RMSE (m³/s)",
                "Peak error (m³/s)", "Timing error (h)", "Volume error (%)"),
  caption = "Average absolute errors for different wavelets and numbers of levels, keeping the same number of detail coefficients."
)
```

## Other methods {#method-other}

As well as the three methods suggested in the lectures, we considered two further methods, each addressing a weakness found above.

### B-splines {#method-bspline}

The polynomial's weaknesses all stem from using a single curve across the whole event, so we also considered a B-spline basis, which joins short cubic pieces smoothly together so that each basis function only affects one part of the hydrograph (Ramsay and Silverman, 2005). The standardised hydrograph is approximated by $y_i(u_j) \approx \theta_{i0} + \sum_{l=1}^{L} \theta_{il}\,B_l(u_j)$, where $B_1, \dots, B_L$ are cubic B-splines with equally spaced knots, and it is fitted and validated in the same way as the polynomial. We chose $L =$ `r n_basis_chosen`, giving `r n_basis_chosen + 1` shape parameters, close to the `r p_chosen + 1` of the polynomial, so that the two can be compared at a similar number of parameters.

### A known hydrograph function {#method-gamma}

The lectures suggest that a known function which approximates hydrographs may give parameters that can be interpreted. We therefore fitted a gamma-type hydrograph (Nash, 1957) with an added baseflow to each extreme flow event by nonlinear least squares, giving three parameters with a physical meaning: the baseflow as a fraction of the peak flow (median `r sprintf("%.2f", median(gamma_params[gamma_ok, "b"]))`), the time of the peak, and the sharpness of the peak.

# Validation of methods

Now that we have chosen the number of parameters for each method, we validate their fits, by checking how well the fitted curves reproduce the observed events. In particular, we consider how the methods perform on contrasting events (the earliest and latest peaks, the shortest and longest durations, and the flattest and sharpest peaks), as well as considering their residuals against time, and parameter correlation.

## Contrasting extreme flow events {#validation-contrast}

```{r all-methods-plot, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 11, fig.height = 10}
plot_all_methods()
```

We observe that the polynomial method underestimates sharp peaks and cannot reproduce events with two peaks, such as events 19, 29 and 41, instead fitting a single peak that is too low and too broad. This is because each polynomial term acts over the whole event, so a sharp change at the peak cannot be made without disrupting the rest of the curve, and a smooth, wide curve is settled on instead. The fitted curve also drifts away from the observed flow at the start and end of the event, because the higher-order terms dominate near the ends of the interval.

The closely related B-spline method fits the recession and the ends of the event closely, but around the peak it shows the same pattern as the polynomial, underestimating sharp peaks and offering only a marginal improvement in capturing events with two peaks. The gamma-type method performs the poorest of the five. This is because, although it matches the height and timing of the main peak, each curve has only a single peak and the same baseflow at the start and end of the event, so it misses one of the peaks of two-peaked events entirely and fits the start and end of most events poorly.

Unlike these three methods, PCA reproduces the single-peak events, 3 and 26, almost exactly, and reproduces events with two peaks closely. For these, the main differences are an underestimate of one of the two peaks, the earlier peak in events 19 and 41 and the later peak in events 2 and 29, and small differences in the recession tail. The wavelet method also reproduces the main body of single-peak events almost exactly, and events with two peaks very closely. However, its fitted curves are jagged in places and show some unrealistic dips and jumps, such as in events 2, 19 and 41. We expect this is because the same detail coefficients are kept for every event, so a coefficient that matters for a particular event may be discarded. There are also sharp deviations at the ends of the interval, likely due to the periodic boundary, which treats the start and end of the curve as joined.

## Residuals

```{r residuals-all, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5}
plot_all_residuals()
```

The residual against time plots (Figure \@ref(fig:residuals-all)) confirm our observations from Subsection \@ref{validation-contrast} across all 41 events. For the polynomial method, the residuals are positive at the peak and negative on either side for most extreme flow events, reinforcing that the fitted peak is systematically too low and too broad, and the drift away from the observed flow at the ends of the interval is clearly visible. The B-spline method shows very similar results around, and at, the peak, however, the residuals are close to zero after $u \approx 0.6$, confirming that the recessions are fitted closely. The gamma-type method has ...

On the other hand, the residuals for PCA are small throughout, and are largest on the rising limb, partly corresponding to underestimates of earlier peaks, such as events 19 and 41. The average residual error is exactly 0 throughout, but this is by construction, because PCA rebuilds each event around the mean curve. The wavelet method also has small residuals throughout, but it is jagged around zero across the whole interval, again reflecting the detail lost when coefficients are not included. The drifting at the ends of the interval is also evident. 

Since the residuals at neighbouring times are correlated, they are not independent, and they need not be normally distributed, but this does not affect our use of the model, as the fitted curve is used as a basis rather than for inference.

The residuals show no systematic pattern, with the average residual close to zero throughout, and are largest on the rising limb, where some events have an earlier, smaller peak. The scores showed no event far from the rest, although on the fourth and sixth components most events lie close to zero with a few lying well away from the centre, which will need to be considered when modelling the variation in the scores between events (Section \@ref(uncertainty)).

In the residuals, the average residual is close to zero except at the end of the event, while a few individual events have larger residuals on the falling limb. The behaviour at the start and end is consistent with the periodic boundaries, which treat the start and end of the hydrograph as joined, even though the flow is different at each.

## Correlation of parameters

Finally, we observe that the coefficients are strongly correlated across extreme flow events, with correlations of up to `r sprintf("%.3f", max(abs(cor(poly_coefs)[upper.tri(cor(poly_coefs))])))` in absolute value, as the powers of $u$ are themselves highly correlated on $[0, 1]$. This means that the coefficients are difficult to interpret and their joint variation between events harder to model, which is a disadvantage of this method for use with an emulator.

Finally, we observe that the shape parameters are correlated across events, with correlations of up to `r sprintf("%.2f", max(abs(cor(wav_params)[upper.tri(cor(wav_params))])))` in absolute value. The strongest correlations are between neighbouring smooth coefficients, since these describe neighbouring parts of the hydrograph, which tend to rise and fall together, while the correlations between the smooth and detail coefficients are mostly weaker. These correlations are smaller than for the polynomial, but unlike the PCA scores, the parameters are not uncorrelated, which makes their joint variation between events harder to model.

Its coefficients are also less strongly correlated than the polynomial's, with correlations of up to `r sprintf("%.2f", max(abs(cor(bspline_coefs)[upper.tri(cor(bspline_coefs))])))` in absolute value.

Gamma-type parameters are close to uncorrelated.
